lead: This unit defines signals and systems, separates continuous-time from discrete-time, and classifies signals by energy, power, periodicity and symmetry. It introduces impulse, step, ramp and exponential models, independent-variable operations, system classes and the four core properties. After it you can test linearity, time invariance, causality and BIBO stability, and treat signals as vectors in an orthogonal signal space.
about: Chapter 1.1 fixes the vocabulary: a signal is a function of an independent variable, a system maps inputs to outputs, and CT and DT signals differ in that variable. Chapter 1.2 classifies signals by energy and power, periodicity and even/odd symmetry. Chapter 1.3 gives the standard models: impulse, step, ramp and exponential, and their relationships. Chapter 1.4 shows independent-variable operations: shift, scale and reversal. Chapter 1.5 classifies CT and DT systems and their block interconnections. Chapter 1.6 tests linearity, time invariance, causality and BIBO stability. Chapter 1.7 treats signals as vectors, defines orthogonal signal space and introduces Parseval's energy relation.

chapters.idea: A signal is a function of an independent variable that carries information, and a system maps input signals to output signals; continuous-time signals use real time t, discrete-time signals use integer index n.
chapters.depth: Define signal, system, input, output and independent variable. Use x(t) for a CT signal and x[n] for a DT signal. A CT signal has a value for every real t; a DT signal has values only at integer n. The amplitude may be voltage, current, temperature or any physical quantity. A system is a black box T that turns x(t) into y(t), or x[n] into y[n]. Some syllabi call a signal a function of one or more independent variables. Give simple examples: speech voltage against time, daily temperature at noon, a share price sampled each day. Show block notation and state that x[n] often comes from sampling but can be native discrete data.

figure.title: From signal to system
figure.aria: A physical temperature goes through a sensor to a continuous-time voltage x(t), then a sampler makes a discrete-time sequence x[n] that a system maps to y[n].

chapters.example: A voltage signal is x(t)=4 sin(20πt) V for CT and x[n]=4 sin(0.2πn) V for DT. State the type of each and compute x(0.025 s) and x[5]. Solution: x(0.025)=4 sin(0.5π)=4 V; x[5]=4 sin(π)=0 V.
chapters.trap: x[n] is not the same as x(nT_s) unless the sequence was made by ideal sampling; n is an integer index, not a time in seconds.
chapters.prereq: Basic trigonometry and functions; no earlier chapter.
chapters.leave: Sampling theorem and reconstruction to Unit 5; Fourier, Laplace and Z transforms to Units 3, 4 and 6.

chapters.idea: A signal is classified by its energy and power, by whether it repeats, and by its even or odd symmetry; these properties decide how it behaves in later transforms.
chapters.depth: Define energy E and average power P for CT and DT signals. For CT: E = ∫<sub>−∞</sub><sup>∞</sup> |x(t)|² dt, P = lim<sub>T→∞</sub> (1/T)∫<sub>−T/2</sub><sup>T/2</sup> |x(t)|² dt. For DT use sums over n. Classify energy signals (finite E, zero P), power signals (finite nonzero P, infinite E) and neither. Define periodic x(t+T)=x(t) with fundamental period T0; DT period N0. Define even x(−t)=x(t) and odd x(−t)=−x(t), with decomposition x_e(t)=(x(t)+x(−t))/2 and x_o(t)=(x(t)−x(−t))/2. Some syllabi call energy and power the size of a signal.

figure.title: Signal classification
figure.aria: A classification tree splits signals into energy or power, periodic or aperiodic, and even or odd, with defining conditions in the notes.

chapters.example: For x(t)=6 cos(200πt)+3 V, find the fundamental period T0, average power P, total energy E, and the even and odd parts. Solution: ω=200π rad/s, so T0=2π/ω=0.01 s. P=6²/2+3²=18+9=27 W; the cross term averages to zero. E is infinite because the signal is periodic and nonzero. The signal is even, so x_e(t)=x(t) and x_o(t)=0.
chapters.trap: A periodic signal with finite amplitude is a power signal, not an energy signal; energy signals have zero average power over all time.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 1 for signal notation and CT/DT distinction.
chapters.leave: Fourier series spectra to Unit 3; correlation and spectral density to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: The standard signals are the impulse, step, ramp and exponential; they are the building blocks from which other signals are written and the test inputs for systems.
chapters.depth: Define CT and DT impulse δ(t), δ[n], unit step u(t), u[n], ramp r(t)=t u(t), r[n]=n u[n], real exponential e^{at} and complex exponential e^{jωt}. This book uses u(0)=1 and u[n]=1 for n≥0. State δ(t) has unit area, δ(t)=0 for t≠0, and δ(0) is not an ordinary value. Give the sifting property ∫x(t)δ(t−t0)dt=x(t0). Give relationships r'(t)=u(t), u'(t)=δ(t) in the generalized sense, and δ[n]=u[n]−u[n−1]. Give the scale rule δ(at)=δ(t)/|a|. Some syllabi call these singularity functions, elementary signals or commonly used signal models. The figure shows u(t), r(t), e^{−t}u(t) and δ(t) at unit amplitude.

figure.aria: A plot shows unit step u(t), unit ramp r(t), decaying exponential e^{-t}u(t), and a unit impulse δ(t) at t=0.

chapters.trap: δ(t) is not a finite-height pulse; its value at t=0 is undefined in ordinary algebra, and only its area and sifting action are used.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 1 for CT/DT notation; Chapter 2 for energy and symmetry.
chapters.leave: Fourier transform of impulse and step to Unit 3; Laplace transform to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: Changing the independent variable shifts, scales or reverses a signal, and combined operations must be read in the correct order.
chapters.depth: For CT: y(t)=x(t−t0) shifts right by t0 for t0>0; y(t)=x(at) compresses for a>1 and expands for 0<a<1; y(t)=x(−t) reverses. For DT: y[n]=x[n−n0] shifts; y[n]=x[Mn] keeps every M-th sample; inserting zeros gives upsampling. Write a combined form as x(at−b)=x(a(t−b/a)): scale by a, then shift right by b/a; or shift right by b, then scale by a. Some syllabi call this transformation of the independent variable or time-domain operations.

figure.aria: A rectangular pulse x(t) from t=0 to 2 is compressed and shifted to x(2t-1) on 0.5 to 1.5, and reversed and shifted to x(-t+1) on -1 to 1.

chapters.example: Given x(t)=2 for 0≤t≤2 and 0 elsewhere, sketch y(t)=x(2t−1) and z(t)=x(−t+1). Solution: y is nonzero when 0≤2t−1≤2, so 0.5≤t≤1.5, with amplitude 2. z is nonzero when 0≤−t+1≤2, so −1≤t≤1, with amplitude 2.
chapters.trap: For x(2t−1), do not shift by 1 and then compress; that gives x(2t−2). The correct inside form is x(2(t−0.5)).
chapters.prereq: Chapter 1 for signal notation; Chapter 3 for step and pulse shapes.
chapters.leave: Convolution to Unit 2; sampling and aliasing to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: A system is an operator that maps an input signal to an output signal, and systems are classified as CT or DT by the independent variable of their inputs and outputs.
chapters.depth: Define a system as T: input set → output set. Write y(t)=T{x(t)} for CT and y[n]=T{x[n]} for DT. Give physical examples: RC circuit, mass-damper system, heating system. Show series and parallel interconnection of blocks. Classify as memoryless or with memory, causal or noncausal, stable or unstable, linear or nonlinear, time-invariant or time-varying, static or dynamic, invertible or noninvertible. Keep the tests for Chapter 6. Some syllabi call this system classification and system as interconnection of elements.

figure.title: CT and DT systems
figure.aria: Two block chains show a continuous-time input x(t) through a CT system to y(t), and a discrete-time input x[n] through a DT system to y[n].

chapters.example: A CT system is y(t)=3x(t)+2 and a DT system is y[n]=x[n]−x[n−1]. Classify each as CT or DT, and as memoryless or with memory. For x(t)=u(t), find y(1); for x[n]=n u[n], find y[2]. Solution: the first is CT and memoryless, with y(1)=3·1+2=5. The second is DT and has memory, with y[2]=2−1=1.
chapters.trap: CT versus DT is about the independent variable, not whether the hardware is analog or digital; a computer can simulate a CT model numerically.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 1 for CT/DT signals; Chapter 3 for standard test inputs.
chapters.leave: Detailed property tests to Chapter 6; convolution and differential equations to Unit 2.

chapters.idea: Linearity, time invariance, causality and BIBO stability are four independent tests on a system, and each test has a direct definition.
chapters.depth: Linearity means additivity and homogeneity: T{a x1+b x2}=a T{x1}+b T{x2} for constants a,b. Time invariance means a shift in input gives the same shift in output: x(t−t0)→y(t−t0). Causality means y(t0) depends only on x(t) for t≤t0. BIBO stability means every bounded input |x(t)|≤Mx gives a bounded output |y(t)|≤My. For an LTI system with impulse response h(t), BIBO stability holds iff ∫|h(t)|dt<∞, and causality holds iff h(t)=0 for t<0; use sums for DT. Some syllabi call this system properties.

figure.title: Property tests
figure.aria: A flowchart starts from a given system and lists separate checks for linearity, time invariance, causality and BIBO stability before a pass or counterexample.

chapters.example: Test y(t)=t x(t) for linearity, time invariance, causality and BIBO stability. Solution: T{a x1+b x2}=t(a x1+b x2)=a t x1+b t x2, so it is linear. Input x(t−t0) gives t x(t−t0), while the shifted output is (t−t0)x(t−t0); these differ for t0≠0, so it is time-varying. The output at t uses x(t) only, so it is causal. For x(t)=M constant, y(t)=Mt is unbounded as t→∞, so it is not BIBO stable.
chapters.trap: Time invariance is not the claim that the system never changes; it is shift equivariance. A nonzero constant term such as +2 breaks linearity.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 5 for the system definition and CT/DT notation; Chapter 3 for impulse response notation.
chapters.leave: LTI impulse response, convolution and differential equations to Unit 2; Laplace and Z stability tests to Units 4 and 6.

chapters.idea: A signal on an interval behaves like a vector: inner products measure similarity, orthogonal functions form a basis, and Parseval's relation gives energy from coefficients.
chapters.depth: Define the CT inner product ⟨x,y⟩=∫ x(t)y*(t)dt over an interval, with y*(t) the complex conjugate; use ⟨x,y⟩=Σ x[n]y*[n] for DT. Define norm ||x||=√⟨x,x⟩ and distance ||x−y||. Two signals are orthogonal when ⟨x,y⟩=0. A set φ_n is orthogonal when ⟨φ_m,φ_n⟩=0 for m≠n, and orthonormal when each also has unit norm. A complete set leaves no nonzero signal orthogonal to all φ_n. For x(t)=Σ c_n φ_n(t), c_n=⟨x,φ_n⟩/⟨φ_n,φ_n⟩. Parseval: ∫|x(t)|²dt=Σ|c_n|²||φ_n||². Some syllabi call this the analogy between vectors and signals, signal space and geometric concepts, or orthogonal signal space.

figure.title: Signal space
figure.aria: A signal and an orthogonal basis set feed inner products, which give coefficients for reconstruction and for Parseval energy.

chapters.example: On the interval 0≤t≤1, φ1(t)=1 and φ2(t)=2t−1. Show they are orthogonal, find ||φ1||² and ||φ2||², and use Parseval to find the energy of x(t)=3φ1(t)+4φ2(t). Solution: ⟨φ1,φ2⟩=∫0^1(2t−1)dt=[t²−t]0^1=0. ||φ1||²=1. ||φ2||²=∫0^1(2t−1)²dt=1/3. Energy=3²·1+4²·(1/3)=9+16/3=43/3≈14.33.
chapters.trap: Orthogonality depends on the interval; φ1 and φ2 are orthogonal on [0,1] but not on [0,2]. For complex signals use the conjugate, and divide by the squared norm when the basis is not unit energy.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2 for energy and power; Chapter 1 for signal notation.
chapters.leave: Fourier series coefficients, Fourier transform and Parseval theorem for those bases to Unit 3; correlation and spectral density to Unit 3.
